state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think the range wouldn't change if all the plants were cut in half or grew by \(3 \mathrm{~cm}\) each? Let's consider how changing all values by the same proportion affects the spread of the data.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I thought that if you cut all the heights in half, the biggest and smallest plants would still be the same distance apart, so the range wouldn't change. And with Katie's example, if you just add \(3 \mathrm{~cm}\) to each height, it seems like the difference between the tallest and shortest would still be the same. But now I'm not sure if that's right. Can you help me understand how the range actually changes?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a scenario where changing all values by the same proportion does affect the range? Consider how the relationship between the heights of the plants might change if they were all doubled or tripled in size. How would that impact the spread of the data?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to address the student's actual misconception (confusing proportion with addition), provides mathematically confusing guidance by conflating these concepts, and the student shows no improvement—remaining confused at the end without resolving their misunderstanding about which operation preserves range.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking and never directly provides the answer, though they could have more effectively used a counterexample to expose the student's flawed reasoning about cutting in half.
